media.title: Hôtel Le Château Frontenac, 54 rue Pierre Charron, Paris — advertisement, 1935
media.description: Advertisement for the Hôtel Le Château Frontenac, 54 rue Pierre Charron, Paris 8e, printed in Le Sport universel illustré on 15 October 1935. It shows the building about a year after Kaper left for the United States, and is used here as a context image of the address rather than as a document of his stay.
media.altText: Black-and-white advertisement showing the exterior of Hôtel Le Château Frontenac at 54 rue Pierre Charron in Paris, with room prices in francs.
media.rightsNote: Reuse rights are not cleared. The advertisement reproduces a photograph of the hotel and was printed in Le Sport universel illustré on 15 October 1935 without a photographer’s or designer’s credit, so it is treated as an anonymous work, for which the French term of seventy years from publication ran out at the end of 2005. It was accordingly still protected in France on 1 January 1996 and the URAA restored United States copyright for ninety-five years from publication, to the end of 2030. Gallica supplies the digitised page under conditions governed by French law, which exclude documents protected by a third party’s copyright and leave reuse in another country to the user. timelineEvents.title: Arrival in New York en route to Los Angeles
timelineEvents.label: 24 Oct 1934 · Arrival in New York
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Kaper arrived in New York from France with Eleonora on a temporary visa, travelling onward to Los Angeles.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper and his wife Eleonora sailed from Le Havre on 17 October 1934 aboard the S.S. Champlain in second cabin class and reached New York on 24 October. Their non-immigrant visas had been issued in Paris on 15 October, numbered in a single series with the Jurmanns’ (NI 1581–1584), and the manifest records Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer as having paid the passage and as the party they were joining in Culver City. Kaper gave his occupation as musician and declared that he meant to stay about eight months and then return, without seeking United States citizenship. David Blum of the Culver Export Corporation met them in New York, and they left for Hollywood on 27 October.
